title: Gateless Barrier, Case 21: Yun-men's Dried Shitstick
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up case 21 of the Mumonkan, in which a monk asks Yunmen "What is Buddha?" and Yunmen answers, "A dried shit stick." Nomon reads Robert Aitken's note linking the stick to the corn cob in his grandparents' outhouse, then tells of wheelbarrowing barrels of feces on an undergraduate biology expedition until the load felt like ordinary stuff. Nomon then turns to Suzuki Roshi, whose special power, as Nomon's teacher put it, was seeing the extraordinary in the ordinary, and reads many short stories from David Chadwick's To Shine One Corner, among them the forgotten shovel, the jelly beans, and the student who begs for enlightenment while Suzuki Roshi sleeps in the car. Nomon closes by returning to Yunmen's answer: a dried shit stick, and everything else.

sentences.text: We're going to continue our exploration of old Zen stories, and tonight is very exciting, because we have reached the famous case 21, from the Mumonkan.
It's another one of the stories where the monk asks a question.
There are different ways to ask it, but the monk essentially asks what is the meaning of practice, what is the meaning of being alive, what is the meaning of Buddha?
It's like the Zen version of our universal question, what is this?
I don't know how we'd say that: what the hell is going on here?
And the teacher answers.
The teacher doesn't exactly answer, really; the teacher responds.
We've heard a variety of responses: three pounds of flax, holding up a finger, "it's just your everyday mind, that's the way."
This is the most fabulous, I think, of all the responses.
So, case 21.
*A monk asked Master Yunmen, "What is Buddha?"
Yunmen replied, "A dried shit stick."* Did I set you up appropriately?
You could read various things into this, as we could into all these stories.
An obvious reading would be everything: everything is Buddha, whether it's clean or dirty, flowers or shit.
You could be curious about aversion.
Is the teacher trying to help us work with our aversion and our desire to have things be really nice and pleasant?
Maybe it was just a simple pointing to an ordinary monastic process.
Apparently in those days, in the toilet, they had these soft sticks, and they might have been peeled, like a little brush.
That's what you would use, and then you'd probably throw it down the hole, I don't know.
In Robert Aitken's commentary on this, he makes a wonderful mention of his grandfather.
Let me see if I can find that.
Yes.
After pages of background on the different teachers involved, Aitken Roshi says:
*Now, about that dried shit stick, it seems that it was a soft stick that was used the way our ancestors used a corn cob in their outhouses.*
I didn't know that.
I guess you'd have a bin full of corn cobs.
If you were growing corn, you'd have a lot of corn cobs.
Anyway, he continues:
*It seems it was used the same way our ancestors used a corn cob in their outhouses.
I'm old enough to remember seeing a withered corn cob on a string in my grandparents' outhouse in Upper Lake, California.
Hanging beside it was an old Sears Roebuck catalog with all the pages torn out.
Beside that was a packet of toilet paper.
It was a time of transition in rural American hygiene.*
I guess in his grandfather's early days they didn't even have any extra corn cobs.
They'd just reuse one, hang it from a stick or from a string.
But another way to look at this, I think, is that not only can we be free from aversion.
I think all of us could tell various stories about shit, and I'll tell mine, just to be thorough.
Aitken explains that his Japanese teacher, Soen Roshi, gave a talk, and all he did was talk about different times he encountered shit, with great glee.
Like anybody, I have some aversion to feces, which is healthy.
It's probably an evolutionary advantage not to want to get too close to a lot of feces, right?
Yeah.
So it's not the worst thing.
It's just a question of being aware of it.
Anyway, I was on a biological field expedition in undergrad: twenty undergrads on the bus with two really wild biology professors.
One of the places we stayed was Granite Mountain Reserve in southeastern California.
It was a designated biological reserve, and there was no infrastructure really.
There was a cabin and an outhouse.
But to prevent impact, after the group had used the outhouse for the three or four or five days we were there, we had to scoop out all the shit, put it in barrels, and haul it away with us.
We had to literally be zero impact, even though we had twenty people there for several days.
I don't know if I volunteered or was volunteered, but I was in charge of the wheelbarrow.
A few other students were in charge of the shovel and the barrel.
Each time I wheelbarrowed a load of our feces from point A to point B, it was a little different experience.
A little bit less gross, a little more ordinary, until eventually it was a lot.
I don't know how we managed to shit that much, actually.
It was a lot, at least in my memory.
Maybe it was only a few trips, but it seemed like fifty trips or something.
By the last trip, I thought, this is just ordinary stuff, ordinary human stuff.
It's neither gross nor lovely.
It's just stuff.
Ever since then, it's been a little easier for me to deal with toilets.
So maybe we should all have such an experience.
But I think the most interesting way to look at this case is to recognize that it's not just that we can tolerate just about anything.
It's that everything in the universe has a deep and fundamental glory to it, a kind of beauty, whether it's shit or stars or flowers or people.
That made me think of Suzuki Roshi, our great-grandfather in the lineage.
At one time I was studying the list of ten great perfect practices.
We usually study a list of six.
These are the paramitas, things like generosity and wisdom and patience.
The longer list includes four more things to practice with great depth, and one of them is special powers.
I thought, well, that's weird.
I thought our whole gig was that we aren't too worried about special powers.
We're just studying our hearts and trying to be more kind and enlightened in a certain way.
Why would we need special powers?
I thought the gig was that the Buddhas renounce special powers.
They don't need them.
So I asked my teacher about this, and he said, well, they always said that Suzuki Roshi's special power was that he saw the extraordinary in the ordinary.
So I think my commentary on Yunmen's dried shit stick will be to read you some stories about Suzuki Roshi.
These are first-person stories, but no authors are given.
They're from a variety of his early students who were talking to David Chadwick, who put this little book together, about what they noticed and remembered about Suzuki Roshi.
It's just a series of little stories.
*One morning, when we were all sitting zazen, Suzuki Roshi gave a brief impromptu talk in which he said, "Each of you is perfect the way you are, and you could use a little improvement."*
One of his favorite sayings.
You're perfect just the way you are.
You really let that sink in.
Like, really?
Me?
Nah.
And you could use a little improvement.
We focus on the improvement part without forgetting about the perfect part.
We're okay.
We're really okay.
And there's work to do, of course.
Next one.
*Once I asked Suzuki Roshi, "What is nirvana?"
He replied, "Seeing one thing through to the end."*
Seeing one thing through to the end.
*One day at Tassajara, Suzuki Roshi and a group of students took some tools and walked up a hot dusty trail to work on a project.
When they got to the top, they discovered they had forgotten a shovel.
The students began to discuss who should return to get it.
After the discussion ended, they looked around and realized Roshi wasn't there.
He was already halfway down the mountain, going down to get the shovel.*
*One time I complained to Suzuki Roshi about the people I worked with.
I found them very unenlightened.
He listened intently.
Finally he said, "If you want to see virtue, you have to have a calm mind."*
If you want to see virtue, you have to have a calm mind.
*It was my first sesshin, which is an intensive Zen meditation retreat.
It was my first sesshin, and before the first day was over, I was convinced I would never make it through.
My husband's turn for dokusan came that afternoon, and he asked Suzuki Roshi to see me instead.
"This is all a mistake," I told Roshi.
"I can't do this.
I just came to be with my husband."
"There is no mistake," he insisted.
"You may leave, of course, but there is no place to go."*
There is no mistake.
You may leave, of course, but there is no place to go.
*A student at Tassajara,* which is our monastery, and one of our dear members, Kate, is there right now.
*A student at Tassajara sat facing Suzuki Roshi on a tatami mat in his room.
The student said he couldn't stop snacking in the kitchen and asked what he should do about that.
Suzuki Roshi reached under his table and said, "Here, have some jelly beans."*
Lots of stories about Suzuki Roshi and food.
The early students were very intense about their diets.
You can mess with them a little bit.
*A student of Suzuki Roshi, a publisher of beat poetry, saw his teacher of a year and a half in a private interview.
He said that he couldn't continue, that every time he sat zazen, he started to cry.
"I can't take it," he said.
"I'm leaving.
I can't be here anymore."
Suzuki Roshi didn't tell him to stay.
He merely said, "You try, and you try, and you fail.
And then you go deeper."*
You try, and you try, and you fail.
And then you go deeper.
This is for our sangha leaders here.
We debate things like this.
*Once a student asked Suzuki Roshi, "Why do you have forty-minute zazen periods when most Zen teachers in America have only thirty?
My legs really hurt if I sit forty minutes.
Won't you consider having thirty-minute periods, at least in sesshin?"
Suzuki replied, "That's very interesting.
I have been thinking we should really have forty-five-minute periods."
After a pregnant pause, he added, "But maybe we can compromise.
Let's make it forty minutes."*
*One day in lecture Suzuki Roshi said, "When you see one leaf falling, you may say, 'Oh, autumn is here.' One leaf is just one leaf.
It means the whole autumn.
Here you are already understanding the all-pervading power of your practice.
Your practice covers everything."*
*When you see one leaf falling, you may say, "Oh, autumn is here."
One leaf is not just one leaf.
It means the whole autumn.
Here you are understanding the all-pervading power of your practice.
Practice covers everything.*
*During a break at one of the early sesshin at Sokoji, a student returned to his seat early in order to straighten a picture on the wall before he sat down on his cushion.
Only he and Suzuki Roshi were in the zendo at that time.
After a moment, Suzuki Roshi got up to leave the room.
He walked down the aisle, stopped at that picture, and returned it to its crooked position, and continued out the door.*
*The student asked, "Does the Zen Master suffer in a different way than his students suffer?"*
*Does the Zen Master suffer in a different way than his students suffer?
Suzuki Roshi answered, "It is the same way.
If not, I don't think he's good enough."*
This is kind of like an answer to the second case.
Remember Baizhang's Fox and karma and suffering?
Good answer for that story.
*During his first dokusan, a student said he couldn't stop thinking during meditation.
Suzuki Roshi asked, "Is there some problem with thinking?"*
*On the fourth day of sesshin...* These are about sesshin.
This guy didn't have much sitting experience, and they're doing these really long days of sitting, so they're really stuck in their memory apparently.
Anyway:

*On the fourth day of sesshin, as we sat with our painful legs, our aching backs, our hopes, our doubts about whether it was all worth it, Suzuki Roshi began to talk during zazen by saying slowly, "The problems you are now experiencing will go away."
We were sure he was going to say, "We'll continue for the rest of your life."
The way he said it, we all laughed.
"The problems you are now experiencing will continue for the rest of your life."*
*One day during a tea break, a student standing next to Suzuki Roshi asked, "So what do you think about all us crazy Zen students?"
Suzuki Roshi said, "I think you're all enlightened until you open your mouth."*
This was a nice one about his generosity.
*Next to the temple on Bush Street was a grocery store run by an old woman.
Suzuki Roshi used to buy the older vegetables that he could find in the bin.
Finally one day the woman said, "Here are some fresh ones, why don't you take the fresh ones?"
"The fresh ones will be bought anyway," he said.
"I'll buy these ones."*
*One morning in the zendo, we were all silently sitting zazen.
Suzuki Roshi said, "Don't move.
Just die over and over.
Don't anticipate.
Nothing can save you now.
This is your last moment.
Not even enlightenment will help you now, because you have no other moments.
With no future, be true to yourself.
And don't move."*
So it's good to practice being really still in the zendo.
Don't move doesn't mean be tense, though, by the way.
*My family and I returned to San Francisco after being away from Zen Center for a year.
When I saw Suzuki Roshi I said, "I think I got a little lost."
He replied, "You can never get lost."*
*A student told Suzuki Roshi about an experience in which he had dissolved into amazing spaciousness.
"Yes, you could call that enlightenment," Suzuki said.
"But it's best to forget it.
How's your work going along?"*
Now and then Suzuki Roshi would make this point.
*In the Lotus Sutra, Buddha says to light up one corner.
Not the whole world.
Light up one corner.
Just make it clear where you are.*
Just make it clear where you are.
That's where David got the title for the book, which is called *To Shine One Corner*.
I think it was originally published with a different title and reissued as this one.
It's supposedly a reference to the Lotus Sutra, but I so far haven't run into that particular part of the Lotus Sutra.
A few more.
Time for a few more, I think.
*A student asked Suzuki Roshi why the Japanese make their teacups so thin and delicate that they break so easily.
"It's not that they're too delicate," he answered, "but you do not know how to handle them.
You must adjust yourself to the environment, and not vice versa."*

*During a formal silent lunch in the zendo, a young woman with a soup tureen stopped in front of Suzuki Roshi, gave him two ladles full, and blurted out, "Suzuki Roshi, when I'm serving you soup, what is it like for you?"
He said, "It's like you are serving your whole being to me in this bowl."*
It's like you're serving your whole being to me in this bowl.
She was breaking protocol.
You're not supposed to talk.
I want to tell Kate this one.
It's about priest practice.
*One Saturday morning, a student arrived late for the beginning of sesshin.

He was Suzuki Roshi's first ordained student and the first one to wear the traditional priest robe, the okesa, in America.* Besides a Japanese priest who had been doing that for years, probably, but anyway, first American.
*After breakfast, Suzuki Roshi took him to task, saying, "Priests don't arrive late.
You're no priest.
You have no right to wear that okesa."
The student was mortified and started to take off his robe.
"What are you doing?" said Suzuki.
"No one has the right to tell you to take off the okesa."*
*During a lecture, Suzuki Roshi said that life was impossible.
"If it's impossible, how can we do it?" a student asked.
"You do it every day," Suzuki answered.*
Sure.
*During a lecture, Suzuki Roshi said that life was impossible.
Life is impossible.
"If it's impossible, how can we do it?" a student asked.
"You do it every day," Suzuki answered.*
*A young woman wearing many strings of beads raised her hand when Suzuki Roshi asked for questions.
"Suzuki Roshi, what is sex?"
"Oh, once you say sex, everything is sex."*
True enough.
*During a formal question and answer ceremony called shosan, Suzuki Roshi responded to a student's question.
The student started to get up from kneeling, and then Suzuki added slowly and deliberately, "The most important thing is to find out what is the most important thing."*
What is the most important thing?
I love this expression.
The most important thing is to find out what is the most important thing.
Just do a couple more.
*As I was telling Suzuki Roshi what a disaster my life had become, he began to chuckle.
I found myself laughing along with him.
There was a pause, and I asked him what I should do.
"Sit zazen," he said.
"Life without zazen is like winding your clock without setting it.
It runs perfectly well, but it doesn't tell time."*
Life without zazen is like winding your clock without setting it.
It runs perfectly well, but it doesn't tell time.
Let me pick a good one.
Oh, this is a good last one.
*While driving my teacher from city center to Tassajara,* which is like a five-hour drive or something, *I said, "Suzuki Roshi, may I ask you a question?"
And he said yes.
So I proceeded to beg him to tell me what I should do to understand reality.
What should I do to become enlightened?
I told him I was totally dedicated to my practice and that whatever he told me I would do, I would do it for sure.
I went on and on, making sure he really understood and was really aware of my sincerity and my devotion.
I turned to him for an answer.
He was sound asleep.*
You have a little flavor of Suzuki Roshi.
I was too young to have met him.
He died in 1971.
My teacher could have, but he didn't get around to it.
He was twenty-five, I guess, when Suzuki Roshi died.
He was a [unclear: "nun and fisher"].
He was living at Berkeley Zen Center, just across the bay.
Occasionally he'd see there was a lecture and he would be too busy to get around to it, and eventually Suzuki Roshi died and there was a big funeral and everything.
Norman says now he regrets he was too self-absorbed or something to go.
So he never saw Suzuki Roshi.
But we know him through his stories.
We get a little sense of his spirit.
What is Buddha?
A dried shit stick.
And everything else, right?
Everything else.
